narrative: Today's notable findings span movement ecology, urban adaptation and deep-time coevolution. Landscape-scale GPS tracking revealed that boreal and Alpine populations of the Eurasian pygmy owl differ sharply in home-range size and daily movement, home ranges roughly twice as large in boreal forests, pointing to context-dependent behavioural flexibility in a forest specialist. Two independent urban studies converged on the same signal: great tits across six European cities show paler carotenoid-based plumage in more impervious territories, while avian functional-trait occupancy of green spaces responded strongly to blue-space allocation, together showing that fine-scale habitat structure, not just overall green cover, shapes urban wildlife. In wildfire country, wolves were shown to actively balance risk and foraging opportunity around active fire fronts and smoke, an unusually direct look at large-carnivore behaviour during fire events. A century of herbarium and photographic records showed flowering phenology responses to warming diverging by season, delaying spring bloomers but advancing autumn-winter ones. On the Canary Islands, a horizon-scanning exercise prioritised the non-native species most likely to become the next invaders, while a Nature Ecology & Evolution review warned that sea-level rise could open a wholly new invasion front for coastal species. In the Everglades, long-term freshwater rehydration has produced diverging marsh productivity trajectories depending on prior drought and fire history, underlining how strongly restoration outcomes are shaped by a site's disturbance legacy. Finally, Cretaceous fossils of a mimicking mantis and Selaginella add rare deep-time evidence for coevolution between insects and plants.
